bug_report_content:
id: 58
status: Fixed
summary: Internet Explorer runtime error after compilation.
labels: ['Type-Defect', 'Priority-Medium']
stars: 4
commentCount: 10
Comment 0 (2009-11-24): What steps will reproduce the problem? See attached HTML file in IE6+ (does not work in IE8 unless Compatibility View is turned *on* for some reason). What is the expected output? What do you see instead? Expected output is on the left-hand side of the page (it is generated by the raw source). Google Closure's output is on the right-hand side of the page. What version of the product are you using? On what operating system? I downloaded compiler-latest.zip today (Nov. 24, 2009, ~ 12:00 PM EST) Please provide any additional information below. There is a variable called "threshold" which is used to generate an array of arrays in the attached HTML file. If it is a small number, IE seems to pass arrays into the sort method (sorting an array of arrays) by value like all other browsers do. But when threshold is large enough (on my machine that happens around 250) IE starts passing the arrays in by value. Google Closure compiler has changed my original source from making local copies to modifying the arguments being passed into the sort comparator ... but as a result of this IE behavior the Closure compiled code breaks.
Comment 1 (2009-11-24): So after looking into this some more, I've learned that arrays are always passed by reference, but that only means you can change attributes and individual items in an array. So for example: var a = [1, 2, 3, 4]; var f = function(x){x = null;}; f(a); // the value of a will remain [1, 2, 3, 4] // but if instead: var g = function(x){x[0] = null;}; g(a); // the value of a is now [null, 2, 3, 4] In the attached example, the Google Closure compiled version is akin to the function f above, which means that the value of the arrays should *not* be changing. In IE, if the threshold is set high enough, however, they do indeed change. So the original report may not be accurate, but this is a real issue.
Comment 2 (2009-11-25): There is definitely something odd occurring here, running it under the debugger with IE7, it reports "Number expected". Adding a "Debug.writeln("blah")" in the "right" spot and the problem goes away: var g_test=function(f,c){ var g=["aaaaaa","bbbbbb"]; c=(function(a,b){ for(var d=[],e=0;e b)}); f.innerHTML=typeof c[0]+" "+c.join(" --- ") };
Comment 3 (2009-11-26): Update summary to something more directly related.
Comment 5 (2010-02-25): I did some research on this issue, documented here: http://www.zachleat.com/web/2010/02/24/array-sort/
Comment 6 (2010-02-25): If you don't want to wait for the compiler fix, just declare the variables outside of the sort, and the compiler won't optimize and reuse them: var a, b; c.sort(function(a1,b1){ a=(a1[1].toUpperCase()); Debug.writeln("Blah"); b=(b1[1].toUpperCase()); return a b)});
Comment 7 (2010-02-26): wow. that's a nice find. i can't imagine what IE could possibly be doing under the covers that would lead to this problem. One possible fix would be to never coalesce the arguments of a function. Another possible fix would be to "fix" Array.prototype.sort: var oldArraySort = Array.prototype.sort; Array.prototype.sort = function(f) { return oldArraySort.call(this, function(x, y) { return f.call(this, x, y); }); }; Neither is really satisfying. Alan, what do you think?
Comment 8 (2010-03-07): Perhaps a @nocoalesce JSDoc tag?
Comment 9 (2010-04-06): fixed by r171
